questions.q: What was the actual root cause of the mass lockout in the Caldera Finance scenario?
options: A syntax error in the KQL query that crashed the automation rule
The script disabling accounts at random instead of by sign-in activity
A shared VPN exit IP matched 38 unrelated employees because the correlation query used only source IP as its criterion
Sentinel failing to raise an alert for the real compromised account
questions.explain: The query was syntactically correct and did exactly what it was told -- the mistake was relying on a shared signal, a VPN exit IP, as the sole match criterion.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the real incident got slower to resolve, not faster, after the automation fired?
options: Because Sentinel stopped generating new alerts after the lockout
Because the SOC spent the next two hours re-enabling 38 unrelated accounts instead of focusing on the one actually compromised account
Because the compromised account was never actually disabled
Because the automation rule required manual restart after every run
questions.explain: The team investigating the real compromise became the same team fielding help-desk tickets and manually restoring access for 38 unrelated employees.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why would a dry-run default alone likely have caught this bug before it caused damage?
options: Dry-run mode automatically fixes incorrect KQL queries
Dry-run mode prevents Sentinel from raising High-severity alerts
Dry-run mode requires a second automation rule to approve the first
A logged 'would disable 39 accounts' message would have been an obviously wrong number for the first human who glanced at it
questions.explain: Logging the intended action instead of executing it turns an invisible mistake into a visible, obviously-wrong number someone would question.

questions.q: Why does the lesson treat a blast-radius cap, a dry-run default, and a human approval gate as three SEPARATE guardrails rather than one idea stated three ways?
options: Because each one independently would have stopped the damage on its own, which is why a team with only one of them could still avoid this outcome
Because only a human approval gate is ever actually necessary
Because Azure requires all three to be configured for compliance reasons
Because dry-run mode and blast-radius caps apply only to AWS, not Azure
questions.explain: The lesson specifically notes that each of the three guardrails independently would have caught the problem -- they're redundant safety layers, not restatements of the same control.

questions.q: What is the lesson's point about 'failing safely vs. failing wide'?
options: Automation should never be used for containment actions under any circumstances
All automation failures are equally acceptable as long as they are logged
Guardrails are only needed if the automation script has a known bug in its code
A flawed correlation rule's damage should be limited by guardrails even when the underlying logic itself is wrong, so it does little instead of a lot
questions.explain: The lesson's conclusion is that good automation doesn't depend on every query being perfect the first time -- it depends on bad logic failing safely instead of failing wide.
